content: 1. The denominator refers to the number of children aged five years included in surveys with HBsAg results. These surveys are designed to measure the prevalence of the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) among children of this age group. Data sources for these surveys may include HBsAg biomarker prevalence surveys, immunization coverage surveys, and administrative vaccination coverage data. 2. The serosurvey sample must be drawn from the specific geographical region being assessed. For example, if the goal is to estimate national childhood HBV transmission, including mother-to-child transmission, the sampling must be geographically representative of the population. Convenience sampling is not acceptable. 3. HBsAg prevalence can be measured among children aged five years, one year, or those aged 1–5 years, depending on the country’s existing surveillance and data collection activities. 4. In regions or countries with a long history of high HBV vaccination coverage and established school-based serosurveys, there may be flexibility to conduct serosurveys among older children beyond five years of age. 5. Data on HBV birth-dose vaccine exposure and completion of the three-dose hepatitis B vaccine series should be obtained from official records. If these records are unavailable, testing for hepatitis B surface antibodies (HBsAb) may be considered for the serosurvey. However, this approach is less preferred due to higher costs but can be used as an additional measure. 6. Specimen collection and transport must be conducted appropriately to minimize bias caused by specimen degradation, particularly in rural and remote areas. Blood specimens for enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) laboratory testing are preferred due to their higher accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) compared to rapid tests. However, in some locations, only rapid tests may be available, and test selection will depend on available resources. 7. When appropriate sampling strategies and sizes are used, along with high-quality testing assays and laboratory procedures, the HBsAg prevalence in the serosurvey should accurately represent the incidence of childhood HBV transmission in the specific geographical region or country for this age group. 8. Other measurement approaches include systematic reviews of peer-reviewed literature reporting hepatitis B prevalence in children under five years of age, followed by modeling to estimate surface antigen prevalence. 9. Disaggregation of data should consider factors such as sampling method, exposure to hepatitis B vaccine birth dose (from official records), completion of the three-dose vaccine series, place of residence, place of birth, sex, and age groups (younger than five years, five years and older). 10. Global reporting platforms include the Sustainable Development Goals, validation of triple elimination (elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HBV, HIV, and syphilis), and validation of hepatitis B elimination and progress toward elimination. 11. The incidence of hepatitis C (HCV) is measured as the estimated number of new HCV infections per 100,000 population per year or per 100 people who inject drugs per year. This indicator tracks progress toward reducing new HCV infections and achieving global health sector strategy targets for hepatitis C elimination by 2030. 12. Evidence-based prevention strategies and highly effective curative treatments for hepatitis C are available. This indicator reflects the outcomes and impacts of hepatitis C prevention and treatment efforts on new HCV infections. It monitors trends, detects shifts in patterns, and projects the epidemic’s future direction. 13. High program coverage of evidence-based prevention measures, such as safe injections in healthcare settings, high-quality blood product testing, harm reduction for people who inject drugs, and access to HCV testing, diagnosis, treatment, and cure, should lead to a decrease in hepatitis C incidence. 14. Global targets include achieving ≤5 new annual HCV infections per 100,000 population and ≤2 new annual HCV infections per 100 people who inject drugs. 15. Direct estimation of hepatitis C incidence can be achieved through prospective cohort studies, retrospective cohort studies, or infectious disease modeling. Prospective cohort studies involve retesting individuals who initially tested negative for HCV antibodies or RNA over time. Retrospective cohort studies use routinely collected health data to identify new HCV cases among individuals who undergo multiple HCV tests as part of routine care. 16. Infectious disease models can estimate hepatitis C incidence using prevalence data and routine programmatic surveillance data. These models are suitable when at least two country-specific prevalence serosurveys and sufficient surveillance data are available to inform model parameters. 17. Additional methods for estimating incidence in specific populations with ongoing risk behaviors include linked repeated cross-sectional surveys. These surveys recruit new participants in each round, and if individual-level data can be linked over time, they can estimate hepatitis C incidence. 18. The mother-to-child transmission rate of HBV measures the proportion of HBsAg-positive infants among those exposed. This indicator assesses the impact of interventions to reduce vertical transmission of HBV. 19. Measuring the mother-to-child transmission rate requires high coverage (>90%) of antenatal HBsAg testing to identify positive mothers and post-vaccination serological testing of exposed infants. Countries providing targeted timely hepatitis B birth-dose vaccines must develop data collection systems and program linkages. 20. Deaths from hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), cirrhosis, and chronic liver diseases attributable to chronic hepatitis B and C are measured to track trends in mortality among individuals with these conditions. This indicator reflects the ultimate outcome of prevention, testing, care, and treatment activities for viral hepatitis. 21. Estimating the fraction of HCC and decompensated cirrhosis attributable to hepatitis B and C involves analyzing medical records from sentinel sites. Mortality data can be retrieved using ICD-10 or ICD-11 codes from national civil registration and vital statistics systems. 22. Global targets include achieving a combined hepatitis Band C-related mortality rate of ≤6 per 100,000 population per year. Data sources include national vital registries, cancer registries, and global disease burden estimates. 23. Disaggregation of data should consider age, sex, HIV status, geographical location, and higher-risk populations. Global reporting platforms include the WHO Global Hepatitis Reporting System and validation of hepatitis B and C elimination.
